title: From the Whole to the Threshold of Personhood
reflection: Carry one of the three things from Module 1 through today, and notice where it changes how you meet an ordinary moment.

questions.q: Which line best sums up Module 1, in Conversation 1.6?
o: The everyday I is observable, so it is not the deepest knower; awareness is alive.
The everyday I is the deepest knower, so a person need look no further than their own thoughts.
The everyday I is an illusion, so a person is wise to ignore what they think and feel in daily life.
The everyday I is a brain event, so a person is wise to leave the question to the scientists.
questions.e: Module 1 reached its view by looking and not by belief: the everyday I can be observed, awareness shines and is alive, its stillness and movement are one, and the One appears as Many within space, time and causation.
questions.c: The everyday I is observable, so not the deepest knower

questions.q: What does the course compare itself to, in Conversation 1.6?
o: A medical education: orientation, anatomy, physiology, clinical framework, treatment.
A language course for the mind: grammar, vocabulary, speaking, writing, and then fluent use.
A military training for the mind: drill, discipline, strategy, battle, and final victory.
A cooking course for the mind: ingredients, recipes, tasting, serving, and the washing up.
questions.e: Module 1 is orientation, Module 2 anatomy, Module 3 physiology, Module 4 the clinical framework, and Module 5 treatment.
questions.c: The course is a medical education for the mind

questions.q: A student asks what Module 2 will cover. Which answer fits Conversation 1.6?
o: The anatomy of the mind: manas, buddhi, ahaṁkāra and citta.
The treatment of the mind: four families of practice, from breath to meditation.
The clinical framework: Ṛta, flourishing and anṛta in everyday life.
The orientation: awareness, stillness, movement and the One and the Many.
questions.e: Module 2 is the anatomy: manas, buddhi, ahaṁkāra and citta. The treatment, the framework and the orientation belong to Modules 5, 4 and 1.
questions.c: Module 2 is the anatomy of the mind

questions.q: “Science and the contemplative traditions are rivals: one of them has to be right and the other wrong.”
questions.e: The lesson speaks of two roads, one dialogue. Science works from outside, by measurement; Yoga and Vedanta from inside, by disciplined attention. Convergences include embodied cognition and Vimarśa, neuroplasticity, relativity and mental time travel.

questions.q: Which pair is named as a convergence in Conversation 1.6?
o: Neuroplasticity and the living power that can wear new grooves, and mental time travel and the mind building time.
Chemistry and the three modes of nature, and astronomy and the passing of the seasons through the year.
Geology and the stages of a life, and weather and the changes of mood in an anxious person's day.
Mathematics and the order of the breath, and music and the numbering of the beats of the heart.
questions.e: The lesson lists embodied cognition and Vimarśa, neuroplasticity, relativity and mental time travel as places where the two roads meet, without claiming that they prove each other.

questions.q: A man says that he cannot see how a lesson on the mind can start with the whole of reality. What does Conversation 1.6 reply?
o: The door to Module 2: localisation, limitation and identification produce the jīva.
The whole is only a poetic opening, so he may skip it and start with the practices of Module 5.
The whole is a belief to be accepted first, so he should take it on trust and then read on.
The whole is a separate subject, so it is not needed in order to follow the later modules.
questions.e: The course starts from the whole so that the person can be understood as a localisation of it. Localisation, limitation and identification produce the jīva, the threshold of personhood.
questions.c: The whole leads to the threshold of personhood

questions.q: A woman asks what to carry from Module 1 into her day. Which answer fits Conversation 1.6?
o: The Self is the awareness in which all appears; patterns of suffering can be remade.
The Self is a belief to hold, and patterns of suffering are fixed once they have been formed.
The Self is the brain, and patterns of suffering are a matter for medicine and no one else.
The Self is the body, and patterns of suffering are best left alone until they pass off.
questions.e: Three things to carry: the Self is the awareness in which everything appears; reality is alive at its core, so suffering patterns can be remade; and the world is real but conditioned, so the haunting past and frightening future are constructions of the present.
questions.c: Carry the Self, the aliveness and the real-but-conditioned world

questions.q: “The conclusions of Module 1 are reached by looking and not by belief.”
questions.e: Each step is an observation that anyone can test: the everyday I can be observed, awareness shines and is alive, stillness and movement can be checked in a single breath. Nothing is asked to be taken on trust.

questions.q: In the Bridge Inquiry, a person is asked to look at their own experience of a hard situation. What is the point of it, in Conversation 1.6?
o: To see for oneself that the observer of the situation is not the situation, and that space opens around it.
To prove that the situation is not real, so that the person can stop being troubled by it at all.
To decide who is to blame for the situation, so that the matter can be put behind them.
To forget the situation for a time, so that the mind can rest and take up something else.
questions.e: The inquiry puts the lesson to use: the one who observes is not what is observed. Nothing is denied; room is made.
questions.c: Observe the situation, and see that the observer is not it

questions.q: A man worries that the Module 1 view makes the world less real. What does Conversation 1.6 say?
o: Real but conditioned: distinctions are real and useful, though not ultimate.
Unreal, and so nothing in it deserves any care, whether it be a person or a promise.
Real and absolute, so that there is nothing deeper than what meets the eye of an observer.
Neither real nor unreal, so that the question is not worth asking by anyone at any time.
questions.e: Māyā does not mean illusion. The world is real, indispensable and conditioned: space, time and causation form the scaffolding of a livable world.
